A session is the unit of continuity in an agent harness. Without one, every turn starts from nothing: the
process forgets the file it just read, the decision it just took, and the question it was halfway through
answering. Persisting the transcript is the cheap half of the fix, because a database write is local and
bounded; the expensive half is deciding what to send back to the provider. Model context windows are finite
and billed by the token, so a harness that replays a whole transcript on every turn eventually pays for the
same history twice, and then pays again. The usual answer is compaction: keep the recent turns verbatim
because they carry the live thread, fold the older turns into one summary because their detail is no longer
load-bearing, and leave the original rows in storage so a later rewind still has raw material to work with.
The threshold that triggers compaction has to be measured, not guessed. Character counts are a usable proxy
when nothing better is available, roughly one token per four characters of English prose, but a provider
that reports usage for the request it just served has already done the counting, and an estimate built on
that number is a fact rather than an approximation. The two only diverge when the heuristic is asked to
extend a reported figure over messages the provider never saw, which is exactly the case the estimator
documents. What matters in practice is that one estimator decides, so the console line and the folded
transcript describe the same event, and that a compaction failure is survivable: the model call that writes
the summary is just another network call, it can fail, and a harness that loses the user's turn because its
own bookkeeping call timed out has made the bookkeeping more important than the work.
